summary: This paper introduces two hybrid error-mitigation methods—Propagated Noise Absorption (PNA) and Euclid—that classically propagate observables through inverted noise channels to construct noise-canceling observables measured on noisy quantum hardware. On a 56-qubit superconducting processor, PNA achieves quadratic sampling cost reduction compared to probabilistic error cancellation while outperforming direct Pauli-propagation simulation of noiseless circuits in the non-Clifford regime.
motivation: Standard Pauli propagation suffers exponential complexity from operator branching that requires truncation, while unbiased error mitigation via probabilistic error cancellation incurs exponentially growing sampling costs. Hybrid approaches can exploit complementary strengths of classical and quantum resources to extend beyond the limits of either alone.
method: Target observables are classically backpropagated through noise-deconvolution maps ($\mathcal{D} = (\mathcal{C}_{\mathrm{ideal}} \mathcal{C}_{\mathrm{noisy}}^{-1})^\dagger$) using antinoise channels. PNA greedily truncates Pauli expansions to $K_E, K_O \in [100, 10000]$ terms; Euclid uses Clifford Perturbation Theory with systematic expansion in sine factors (bubble and step diagrams) up to order $K \in [2, 4, 6]$. The resulting modified observable $\tilde{O}$ is measured on the noisy QPU.
result: On 20-qubit numerics with $\theta = 0.25$, PNA with $K_E = K_O = 10^4$ removes truncation bias to shot-noise level where direct Pauli propagation to $10^9$ terms shows bias $\approx 10\times$ larger. On 56-qubit hardware experiments at EPLG $\approx 2 \times 10^{-3}$, PNA sampling cost scales as the square root of shaded-lightcone PEC cost across non-Clifford angles, confirming expected quadratic speedup, with residual error dominated by noise-model inaccuracy at Clifford points ($\theta = 0, \pi/2$).
